{{short description|Describes a property of the cevians of a triangle intersecting in a common point}}
[[File:Satz von Reuschle3.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Reuschle's theorem:<br/> cevians <math>AP_a</math>, <math>AP_b</math> and <math>AP_c</math> intersect in <math>D</math> <br/> <math>AP'_a</math>, <math>AP'_b</math> and <math>AP'_c</math> intersect in <math>D'</math>]]
In elementary geometry, '''Reuschle's theorem''' describes a property of the [[cevian]]s of a triangle intersecting in a common point and is named after the German mathematician [[Karl Gustav Reuschle]] (1812–1875). It is also known as '''Terquem's theorem''' after the French mathematician [[Olry Terquem]] (1782–1862), who published it in 1842.

In a triangle <math>ABC</math> with its three cevians intersecting in a common point other than the vertices <math>A</math>, <math>B</math> or <math>C</math> let <math>P_a</math>, <math>P_b</math> and <math>P_c</math> denote the intersections of the (extended) triangle sides and the cevians. The circle defined by the three points <math>P_a</math>, <math>P_b</math> and <math>P_c</math> intersects the (extended) triangle sides in the (additional) points <math>P'_a</math>, <math>P'_b</math> and <math>P'_c</math>. Reuschle's theorem now states that the three new cevians <math>AP'_a</math>, <math>BP'_b</math> and <math>CP'_c</math> intersect in a common point as well.
